subject: Medicine
summary: Iron deficiency anaemia is a common microcytic, hypochromic disorder caused by inadequate iron intake, absorption or chronic loss. It presents with fatigue, pallor and sometimes shortness of breath. Diagnosis relies on CBC, ferritin and transferrin receptor levels.

sections.p: Iron deficiency anaemia (IDA) is defined by low haemoglobin with microcytosis and hypochromia, confirmed by low ferritin (<15 µg/L) or high soluble transferrin receptor (sTfR).

t.b: Shows low Hb, MCV <80 fL, low MCH – indicates microcytosis
Low ferritin (<15 µg/L) confirms iron depletion; high ferritin (>200 µg/L) rules out IDA

sections.p: Severity is graded by haemoglobin: mild (10–11.9 g/dL), moderate (7–9.9 g/dL), severe (<7 g/dL).
In low‑resource settings, the top causes are nutritional deficiency, chronic blood loss, and parasitic infection.
Patients report fatigue, pallor, dyspnoea on exertion, and sometimes a sore tongue or restless legs. Children may have growth delay.
Key tests assess iron status and rule out mimics. Use CBC, ferritin, sTfR, and CRP if inflammation is suspected.

t.b: Detects microcytosis and hypochromia – first clue
Low ferritin confirms iron depletion; high ferritin suggests inflammation or overload
High sTfR indicates iron demand; normal sTfR with low ferritin suggests anemia of chronic disease
Elevated values point to inflammation, which can raise ferritin independently of iron stores

sections.p: Severe anaemia can cause tachycardia, syncope, heart failure, and increased mortality. Untreated IDA may worsen infections and impair cognition.
Treat the underlying cause, provide iron supplementation, and monitor response. Oral ferrous sulfate is first line; parenteral iron is reserved for malabsorption or intolerance.
b: Oral ferrous sulfate – improves iron stores and corrects anaemia

t.b: Avoid high-dose iron in patients with active bleeding or infection due to risk of oxidative damage
Monitor for hypersensitivity and iron overload

sections.p: Repeat CBC and ferritin after 4–6 weeks to assess response. Preventive strategies include iron‑fortified foods, deworming, and maternal supplementation.
b: Re‑check Hb and ferritin 4–6 weeks post‑therapy

sections.p: IDA mimics include thalassemia trait, anemia of chronic disease, sideroblastic anaemia, and lead poisoning.
b: Thalassemia trait – normal ferritin, normal sTfR

t.b: Normal in IDA; elevated in diabetes

sections.p: Inflammation raises ferritin, masking IDA. GI bleeding may not show obvious blood loss. Low sTfR can be seen in liver disease.
b: High ferritin in infection or liver disease

whenToSeekHelp: Chest pain or shortness of breath at rest

faq.a: Yes, iron can irritate the gut; taking with food or switching to a different formulation may help.

faq.q: Is ferritin always low in iron deficiency?
faq.a: Not if there is inflammation; ferritin can be normal or high, so sTfR or transferrin saturation should be checked.

faq.q: Can children with iron deficiency develop behavioural problems?
faq.a: Yes, iron is essential for brain development; deficiency can lead to attention difficulties and poor school performance.

exam: Explain why ferritin is a better marker than transferrin saturation in low‑resource settings.
Describe the diagnostic work‑up for a 25‑year‑old woman with microcytic anaemia and heavy menstrual bleeding.
Outline the first‑line treatment for a child with iron deficiency anaemia in a rural clinic and how you would monitor response.
